summary: Psalm 48 praises Yahweh in connection with Zion, the city of God, and describes the city as beautiful, secure, and joyful. Enemy kings assemble but are terrified and flee, while the worshiping community reflects on God's loving kindness in the temple. The psalm ends by telling people to inspect Zion's defenses and pass on the testimony that God will guide his people.
whyItMatters: This chapter is one of the Psalms' songs of Zion: it joins praise of God to the visible city, temple, and remembered protection of Jerusalem. Inside Book II of Psalms, it gives communal words for confidence in God without turning the city itself into an independent source of security.

context.author: Associated in its heading with the sons of Korah; Psalms as a whole is a many-writer anthology, and the precise meaning of such headings is debated.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the psalm as Scripture.
context.date: The individual psalms come from varied periods, and the final five-book Psalter is a later anthology; this psalm cannot be dated securely from this chapter alone.
context.setting: Zion, the city of God, and the temple are central images; the poem is located within Book II of Psalms, chapters 42-72.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and public praise, using compressed images, parallel lines, and communal memory.

outline.heading: Praise in the city of God
outline.note: The psalm opens by praising Yahweh in his holy mountain and describing Mount Zion as the city of the great King where God is known as refuge.

outline.heading: Kings panic and flee
outline.note: A group of kings gathers, sees the city, and is overwhelmed with fear; the image of ships broken by an east wind widens the scene of divine power.

outline.heading: Heard and seen
outline.note: The community says that what it had heard about God's city has now been seen, and it confesses that God will establish it forever.

outline.heading: Praise in the temple
outline.note: The worshipers think about God's loving kindness in the temple and connect God's name, praise, righteousness, and judgments with Zion's joy.

outline.heading: Tell the next generation
outline.note: The psalm invites people to walk around Zion, observe its defenses, and pass on the claim that this God is their God and guide.

keyVerses.text: A Song. A Psalm by the sons of Korah. Great is Yahweh, and greatly to be praised, in the city of our God, in his holy mountain.
keyVerses.why: This opening identifies the poem as praise and joins Yahweh's greatness to the city and holy mountain that dominate the chapter.

keyVerses.text: God has shown himself in her citadels as a refuge.
keyVerses.why: The verse states the chapter's central confidence: the city's safety is explained by God's presence, not by walls alone.

keyVerses.text: As we have heard, so we have seen, in the city of Yahweh of Armies, in the city of our God. God will establish it forever. Selah.
keyVerses.why: This verse turns inherited testimony into present witness and marks the poem's confidence that God establishes the city.

keyVerses.text: For this God is our God forever and ever. He will be our guide even to death.
keyVerses.why: The final line moves from Zion's visible strength to a lasting confession about God as guide.

themes: praise reaching the ends of the earth

questions.question: What is Mount Zion in this chapter?
questions.answer: In this psalm, Mount Zion is the holy mountain and the city of the great King. The chapter treats it as the place where God's presence, praise, temple, and protection are seen together.

questions.question: Does the psalm praise the city or God?
questions.answer: It praises God, but it does so through the language of the city. Zion is beautiful and secure because God is known there as refuge and because the city belongs to God.

questions.question: Who are the kings in verses 4-6?
questions.answer: The chapter does not name them. It only says that kings assembled, saw the city, became amazed and dismayed, and hurried away. Readers may compare other biblical battle or rescue texts, but this psalm itself keeps the scene compressed and unnamed.

questions.question: What is hard about the claim that God will establish the city forever?
questions.answer: The verse makes a strong claim about God's establishing the city. Readers differ over how to hear this after later biblical history includes Jerusalem's destruction and exile: some emphasize the psalm's liturgical confidence in God's rule, while others also trace later hopes beyond the physical city's vulnerable history. The chapter itself states the confidence without explaining later events.

questions.question: Why mention the ships of Tarshish?
questions.answer: The image shows power being broken by an east wind. The psalm does not explain the ships in detail, but it uses them as a vivid picture of something impressive and distant being shattered by God's action.

questions.question: What happens in the temple in this psalm?
questions.answer: The worshipers think about God's loving kindness in the middle of the temple. The verse presents temple worship as reflection on God's character, not only as a place or ritual setting.

questions.question: Why does the psalm tell people to walk around Zion and count towers?
questions.answer: The command invites inspection and remembrance. The people are to notice the city's towers, bulwarks, and palaces so they can tell the next generation what they have seen.

questions.question: What are the daughters of Judah?
questions.answer: The phrase is a poetic way of speaking about Judah's communities or people rejoicing. The psalm pairs Mount Zion being glad with the daughters of Judah rejoicing because of God's judgments.

questions.question: How does the last verse change the focus?
questions.answer: After the invitation to inspect Zion, the psalm ends by confessing who God is: 'our God forever and ever.' The final emphasis is not only on the city standing, but on God guiding his people even to death.

glossary.def: The mountain and city at the center of the psalm's praise; the chapter calls people to rejoice in it and walk around it.
Fortified parts of the city; the psalm says God has shown himself there as a refuge.
A preserved performance marker in Psalms whose exact ancient function is uncertain.
Defensive structures of Zion that the people are told to notice before telling the next generation.
